November 25, 2026 
 
RBI Bulletin – November 2026 
 
     Today, the Reserve Bank released the November 2026 issue of its monthly Bulletin. 
The Bulletin includes six speeches, four articles and current statistics. 
 
     The four articles are: I. State of the Economy; II. Shifting Drivers of Imported 
Inflation: COVID-19 Pandemic to the West Asia Conflict; III. Performance of the NBFC 
Sector during 2025-26: A Review; and IV. Disentangling the Impact of US Monetary 
Policy on Indian Financial Markets: An Event Study Approach.  
 
I. State of the Economy 
 
     Supply side challenges, elevated energy prices, and geopolitical uncertainty 
remain significant headwinds to the global economic outlook. Persistent inflationary 
pressures have led to synchronised monetary policy tightening across major central 
banks in the last three months. Pullback in AI-related stocks and elevated sovereign 
bond yields, despite some softening from multi-decade highs, remain a source of 
volatility in financial markets. Amidst uneven economic performance globally, the 
Indian economy stood out. High-frequency indicators of domestic economic activity 
showed resilience in October, underpinned by strong credit demand. Headline CPI 
inflation inched up, primarily driven by higher food inflation. With strong exports 
performance, the trade deficit narrowed in October as compared to corresponding 
month of the previous year. Equity markets rebounded supported by robust corporate 
earnings and foreign portfolio inflows. Net inflows under ECB and NRI deposits also 
remained strong. 
 
II. Shifting Drivers of Imported Inflation: COVID-19 Pandemic to the West Asia 
Conflict  
 
By Snehal S. Herwadkar, Ishu Thakur, Abhiruchi Rathi, Paras and Parul Arora 
 
     This article examines how successive global shocks have reshaped the drivers of 
imported inflation in India. It constructs an import-intensity-weighted consumer price 
index (CPI) using item-level production, imports and exports data to assess the 
contribution of imported items to retail inflation. The analysis finds that food and fuel 
were the principal channels through which imported inflation impacted retail inflation

Governor, Reserve Bank of India meets Managing Directors & Chief Executive 
Officers of select NBFCs, HFCs and Industry Representatives in Mumbai on 
November 23, 2026 
     As part of the Reserve Bank’s ongoing engagement with regulated entities, the 
Governor, Reserve Bank of India, today met in Mumbai with the Managing Directors and 
Chief Executive Officers (MDs & CEOs) of select Non-Banking Financial Companies 
(NBFCs), including Government NBFCs, Housing Finance Companies (HFCs) and 
Microfinance Institutions. 
     Representatives of Sa-Dhan, the Micro Finance Institutions Network (MFIN) and the 
Finance Industry Development Council (FIDC) also participated. 
     Deputy Governors Shri Swaminathan J., Dr Poonam Gupta, Shri S. C. Murmu and 
Shri Rohit Jain attended the meeting, along with other senior officers of the Reserve Bank. 
The MD & CEO of the National Housing Bank also participated. 
     The Governor acknowledged the role of NBFCs and HFCs in supporting economic 
activity by widening access to credit. He emphasised the need for responsible and 
sustainable credit growth and urged NBFCs to put customers first as they expand their 
business. He highlighted the importance of quality service, effective grievance redressal 
and fair recovery practices. He also encouraged NBFCs to use the Central KYC Records 
Registry (CKYCR) for customer onboarding and to keep customer records in the registry 
up to date to improve customer convenience. 
     The Governor urged participants to strengthen their cybersecurity infrastructure and 
adopt a comprehensive, risk-based approach to managing cyber and IT risks, with 
appropriate oversight by their boards and senior management. 
     Participants shared feedback on policy and operational matters concerning the NBFC 
sector.

ANNEX 
Type of Auction 
1. For multiple price-based auction, successful bids will get accepted at the respective 
quoted yield/price for the security. For uniform price-based auction, bids will get 
accepted at the cut off yield/price accepted in the auction.  
2. The auction will be yield based for new security and price based for securities which 
are re-issued.  
3. In case of a Floating Rate Bonds (FRB), the auction will be spread-based for new 
security and price based for securities which are reissued. At the time of placing bids 
for new FRB, the spread should be quoted in percentage terms.  
Minimum Bid Size 
4. The securities will be issued for a minimum amount of ₹10,000/- (nominal) and in 
multiples of ₹10,000/- thereafter.   
Non-Competitive Segment 
5. In all the auctions, Government security up to 5% of the notified amount for sale of 
individual security will be allotted to the eligible individuals and institutions under the 
Scheme for Non-competitive Bidding Facility in the Auctions of Government 
Securities. Individual investors can also place bids as per the non-competitive 
scheme through the Retail Direct portal (https://rbiretaildirect.org.in). 
6. Each bank or Primary Dealer (PD) on the basis of firm orders received from their 
constituents will submit a single consolidated non-competitive bid for individual 
security on behalf of its constituents in electronic format on the Reserve Bank of India 
Core Banking Solution (e-Kuber system).  
7. Allotment under the non-competitive segment will be at the weighted average rate of 
yield/price of the successful bids that will emerge in the auction on the basis of the 
competitive bidding. 
Submission of Bids 
8. Both competitive and non-competitive bids for the auction should be submitted in 
electronic format on the Reserve Bank of India Core Banking Solution (e-Kuber 
system).  
9. Bids in physical form will not be accepted except in extraordinary circumstances.

should be submitted to the Public Debt Office, Mumbai through (email; Phone no:

12. For other auction related difficulties, IDMD auction team can be contacted (email; 
Phone no: 022-22702431, 022-22705125). 
 
 
 
 
Multiple Bids 
13. An investor can submit more than one competitive bid in electronic format on the 
Reserve Bank of India Core Banking Solution (e-Kuber system).  
14. The aggregate amount of bids submitted by an investor in an auction should not 
exceed the notified amount of auction.   
Decision Making Process 
15. On the basis of bids received, the Reserve Bank will determine the minimum 
price/maximum yield up to which tenders for purchase of Government Security will 
be accepted at the auctions.  
16. Bids quoted at rates lower than the minimum price/higher than the maximum yield 
determined by the Reserve Bank of India will be rejected.  
17. Reserve Bank of India will have the full discretion to accept or reject any or all bids 
either wholly or partially without assigning any reason.

Ledger Account (SGL) or to Constituents’ Subsidiary General Ledger Account 
(CSGL), maintained with Reserve Bank of India.

case of securities with non-standard maturities. The exact periodicity of coupon

23. Investments by Non-Residents are subject to the guidelines on ‘Fully Accessible 
Route’ for Investment by Non-residents in Government Securities and other related 
guidelines as issued by the Reserve Bank from time to time.

November 23, 2026 
 
RBI issues Draft Amendment Directions for ‘Preventive Safeguards for 
Electronic Banking Transactions (EBTs)’ 
 
     The Reserve Bank had issued the Amendment Directions dated June 24, 
2026 on ‘Customer Protection in Fraudulent Electronic Banking 
Transactions’ which, inter alia, strengthened the existing framework for limiting 
liability of customers in unauthorised Electronic Banking Transactions (EBTs). 
While the revised framework primarily addresses customer liability in the event of 
fraudulent EBTs, a need is felt to strengthen the same from a preventive 
perspective by providing customers with greater control over the manner and 
extent to which digital payment channels may be used. 
  
     Further, on a review to bring in uniformity in practices adopted by banks and 
ensure that customers are protected against specific acts of omission or 
commission on part of the banks, it has been decided to expand the scope of the 
definition of ‘negligence by a bank’ specified in the aforementioned Amendment 
Directions. 
 
2. Accordingly, the Reserve Bank has today issued the following draft 
Amendment Directions for public comments, which propose to amend Directions 
on Responsible Business Conduct issued by the Department of Regulation, RBI:

RBI releases 2026 list of Domestic Systemically Important Banks (D-SIBs) 
 
     State Bank of India, HDFC Bank, and ICICI Bank continue to be identified as 
Domestic Systemically Important Banks (D-SIBs) under the same bucketing structure 
as in the 2025 list of D-SIBs. The additional Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) requirement 
for these D-SIBs will be in addition to the capital conservation buffer.

Background: 
 
     The Reserve Bank had issued the Framework for dealing with Domestic 
Systemically Important Banks (D-SIBs) on July 22, 2014, which was subsequently 
updated on December 28, 2023. The D-SIB framework requires the Reserve Bank to 
disclose the names of banks designated as D-SIBs starting from 2015 and place these 
banks in appropriate buckets depending upon their Systemic Importance Scores 
(SISs). Based on the bucket in which a D-SIB is placed, an additional common equity 
requirement has to be applied to it. In case a foreign bank having branch presence in 
India is a Global Systemically Important Bank (G-SIB), it has to maintain additional 
CET1 capital surcharge in India as applicable to it as a G-SIB, proportionate to its Risk 
Weighted Assets (RWAs) in India, i.e., additional CET1 buffer prescribed by the home 
regulator (amount) multiplied by India RWA as per consolidated global Group books 
divided by total consolidated global Group RWA. 
 
     The Reserve Bank had announced SBI and ICICI Bank as D-SIBs in 2015 and 
2016 while HDFC Bank was classified as D-SIB in 2017 along with SBI and ICICI

Annex 
Operational Guidelines for Switch/Conversion Transactions of State Government 
Securities 
Switch module on e-Kuber 
1.  The market participants can bid in the switch auction through the Switch Transaction 
module provided in the e-Kuber portal. 
Bidding in a switch transaction 
2. Bidding in the auction implies that the market participants agree to sell the source 
security/ies to the respective State Government and simultaneously agree to buy the 
destination security from the same State Government at their respective quoted prices. 
Placing of bids 
 
3. Each bid should specify the following details: 
 
I. 
Amount of the source security (Face Value) that the participants are willing to sell. 
II. 
Price of the source security (expressed up to two decimal places). 
III. 
Choice of destination security and the price of the destination security (expressed up 
to two decimal places), at which the participants are willing to buy the destination 
security. 
4. The participants can choose to bid for any/all the destination security/ies, but the aggregate 
amount of bids for the source security should not exceed their holdings of the source security 
in face value terms.   
Minimum Bid size 
5. Minimum bid size would be ₹10,000 and in multiples of ₹10,000 thereafter. The participants 
are allowed to submit multiple bids. However, the aggregate amount of bids submitted should 
not exceed the notified amount of source security/basket of source securities in the auction.  
Price of source security 
6. The price of the source security quoted must be equal to the FBIL closing price of the 
source security as on the previous working day. 
7. Bids for source security not as per the price mentioned above will be rejected.  
Price of destination security 
8. Bids for the destination security may be placed after taking into account the price of source 
security as mentioned above.  
Method of auction 
9. The auction will be a multiple-price based auction, i.e. successful bids will get accepted at 
their respective quoted prices for the source and destination securities. 
Auction decision 
10. The auction cut-off will be decided based on the price of the destination security/ies. 
11. Successful bidders are those who have placed their bids at or above the cut-off price. All 
bids lower than the cut-off price will be rejected. 
12. There will be provision of pro-rata allotment, should there be more than one successful bid 
at the cut-off price.  
 
 
 
Amount of destination security and dealing in odd amounts during switch auction 
13. The switch ratio, which is the ratio of the price of the source security to the price of the 
destination security, would be rounded off at 8 decimal places. 
14. The amount of destination security to be issued for each successful bid will be computed 
by multiplying the allotted amount (FV) of the source security with the rounded-off switch ratio. 
The amount of destination security (FV) would be rounded-off to the nearest lower value in 
multiples of ₹10,000.  
15.The odd amount of destination securities (less than ₹10,000) which has been rounded-off, 
would be notionally allotted and bought back from the bidders at the quoted bid price of the 
destination security. The net cash consideration to be paid to the bidder for such odd amounts 
would be the clean price of these securities (as the accrued interest received during notional 
allotment and paid during notional buyback offset each other). 
Fund settlement 
16. Though the conversion would be broadly cash neutral, there will be fund settlement for the 
net accrued interest (accrued interest for the source security FV – accrued interest for the 
destination security FV) for each bid. Cash consideration (due to rounding-off of face value of 
destination security) computed for each bid would be added to the net accrued interest.  
Accordingly, fund settlement will be done for the final amount (Net accrued interest + cash 
consideration) for each bid.

November 20, 2026 
RBI imposes monetary penalty on Fusion Finance Limited 
     The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has, by an order dated November 17, 2026, 
imposed a monetary penalty of ₹7.50 lakh (Rupees Seven Lakh Fifty Thousand only) 
on Fusion Finance Limited (the company) for non-compliance with certain provisions of 
directions issued by RBI on ‘Know Your Customer (KYC)’ and ‘Internal Ombudsman’. 
This penalty has been imposed in exercise of powers conferred on RBI under section 
58G(1)(b) read with section 58B(5)(aa) of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934. 
     The statutory inspection of the company was conducted by RBI with reference to its 
financial position as on March 31, 2026. Based on the supervisory findings of non-
compliance with RBI directions and related correspondence in that regard, a notice was 
issued to the company advising it to show cause as to why penalty should not be 
imposed on it for failure to comply with the RBI directions. 
     After considering the company's reply to the notice, additional submissions made by 
it and oral submissions made during the personal hearing, RBI found that the following 
charges against the company were sustained, warranting imposition of monetary 
penalty: 
i. 
The company failed to obtain PAN or equivalent e-document thereof or Form 60 
from customers, while establishing an account-based relationship with those 
customers; and, 
ii. 
The company failed to escalate the partly or wholly rejected complaints to the 
Internal Ombudsman for a final decision within the prescribed time.  
     This action is based on deficiencies in regulatory compliance and is not intended to 
pronounce upon the validity of any transaction or agreement entered into by the 
company with its customers. Further, imposition of this monetary penalty is without 
prejudice to any other action that may be initiated by RBI against the company.

November 19, 2026 
 
Finances of Panchayati Raj Institutions 
 
     Today, the Reserve Bank released the second edition of its biennial Report titled 
“Finances of Panchayati Raj Institutions”. The theme of this edition is ‘Local Finances and 
Capacity Building in Rural India’. Drawing upon a balanced panel of 2.25 lakh Gram 
Panchayats for the period 2022-23 to 2024-25, the Report presents an assessment of their 
finances and their role in achieving sustainable and inclusive rural socio-economic 
development. 
 
Highlights:  
 
• Gram Panchayat finances strengthened during 2022-23 and 2023-24; they, however, 
remain dependent on intergovernmental transfers, accounting for about 90 per cent of 
total receipts, while own source revenues (OSR) accounted for a modest share of 
about 10 per cent, predominantly driven by non-tax receipts such as interest receipts, 
Panchayati Raj programme funds and user charges.  
• Expenditure patterns primarily reflected both the mandates of the Fifteenth Finance 
Commission and convergence with national schemes/missions, with water supply and 
sanitation accounting for the largest share (about 40 per cent) of total expenditure. 
• While notable progress has been made in rural connectivity, electrification, water 
supply, sanitation and community assets, inter-State disparities persist in access, 
quality and functionality.  
• As some large Gram Panchayats transition to small urban local bodies or Town 
Panchayats, functional responsibilities may expand faster than fiscal and 
administrative preparedness, requiring transitional fiscal support and administrative 
capacity building alongside a calibrated strengthening of OSR through improved 
collection efficiency and rationalised property taxes and license fees. 
 
     This Report has been prepared in the Division of Local Finances of the Department of 
Economic and Policy Research. The current edition, along with the previous edition of the 
Report, is available on the Reserve Bank’s website (www.rbi.org.in). Feedback and 
comments to help improve the analytical and informational content of the Report may be 
sent to the Director, Division of Local Finances, Department of Economic and Policy 
Research, Amar Building (6th Floor), Reserve Bank of India, Sir Pherozshah Mehta Road, 
Mumbai – 400 001 or through e-mail.
